title: Checkpoint: The Tools of Astronomy
objective: After this level you can match each kind of light and instrument to what it lets astronomers study.
summary: Each wavelength needs its own tools: radio dishes, infrared and X-ray telescopes in space, and spacecraft that go and look.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale. One sky, many kinds of light.
cards.body: Every kind of light shows something the others miss. You've met radio, infrared and visible light. One more, and then the full toolkit.

cards.headline: X-rays: the hottest things
cards.body: X-ray telescopes reveal extremely hot gas, like the gas around black holes. There's a catch, and you met it in Level 34: Earth's atmosphere absorbs X-rays. So X-ray telescopes must work in space. NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory launched in 1999 to do exactly that. The same air that blinds X-ray astronomers on the ground is shielding you from X-rays right now.

cards.headline: Match the light to the job
Or just go there
cards.body: Some questions can't be answered from a distance, so we sent robots and people. Voyager 2 flew past Uranus and Neptune, still the only spacecraft to visit either. Apollo astronauts carried 382 kg of the Moon home to study. Telescopes collect the light. Sometimes you go and collect the rocks.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: X-ray telescopes see extremely hot gas, only from space
Radio passes through dust; infrared sees star birth
Spectra reveal what stars are made of
Each wavelength needs its own tools

questions.prompt: What do spectral lines tell astronomers about a star?

options.label: How old the star is
Which elements the star contains
How far away the star is
options.rationale: Distance comes from other methods, like parallax.

options.label: How many planets orbit it

questions.explanation: Each element leaves its own lines, so a spectrum reveals a star’s composition.

questions.prompt: Which kind of telescope can observe through clouds and in daylight?

options.label: An X-ray telescope on the ground
An optical reflector on a mountain
options.rationale: Clouds and daylight stop optical telescopes.

options.label: A radio telescope
An ultraviolet telescope at sea level

questions.explanation: Radio waves pass through clouds and dust, and radio telescopes can observe during the day.

questions.prompt: An astronomer wants to study the extremely hot gas around a black hole. Which tool fits best?

options.label: A radio telescope in a desert
options.rationale: Radio is better for cooler gas and dust.

options.label: A small refracting telescope
options.rationale: Visible light won’t show that hot gas well.

options.label: An infrared telescope inside a dust cloud
options.rationale: Infrared suits dust and cool objects.

options.label: An X-ray telescope in space, like Chandra

questions.explanation: Extremely hot gas glows in X-rays, and only space telescopes can see X-rays.

questions.prompt: Why was Hubble placed above Earth’s atmosphere?

options.label: To escape blurring and see light the air blocks
To get much closer to the stars
options.rationale: A few hundred km makes no difference to star distances.

options.label: To escape the pull of Earth’s gravity
options.rationale: Hubble orbits Earth; gravity still holds it.

options.label: To travel onward to other planets
options.rationale: It stays in orbit around Earth.

questions.explanation: Above the atmosphere, Hubble avoids blurring and can see ultraviolet light that never reaches the ground.

questions.prompt: Chapter 4 recap: which pairing of tool and discovery is correct?

options.label: Radio telescope → Galileo’s moons of Jupiter
X-ray telescope → Helium in the Sun
options.rationale: Helium was found in the Sun’s visible spectrum.

options.label: Spectroscope → helium found in the Sun
Infrared telescope → the first Moon rocks
options.rationale: Moon rocks came back with Apollo astronauts.

questions.explanation: Helium was discovered in 1868 as a line in the Sun’s spectrum, before it was found on Earth.
